What does the
map reveal?

Indian art has many centres. Shelters and monasteries preserve early visual stories; temples and courts supported specialist workshops; communities sustain living crafts; modern schools and cities create new artistic networks. Geography helps explain their differences, while patronage, religion, migration and cultural exchange help explain their connections. These twelve examples are a starting point, not a complete history.

About this atlas

The assignment

Create an interactive digital map that connects important places in Indian art history with images or image links, short descriptions, historical context, artists and artworks. Each location also includes fuller notes on materials, technique, subjects and visual interpretation. The purpose is to understand the geographic spread and influence of art styles. This atlas meets that brief through twelve clickable locations and their source records.

How to explore

Click a numbered pin or a location in the list. Search by place, style, artist or keyword, or filter by region and period/tradition. “Previous” and “Next” step through the visible selection. Zoom controls magnify the selected location; the home button restores the whole map. All core features work without internet. External sources and image galleries require a connection.

How the history is presented

Dates describe a selected work, phase or institutional milestone, not the lifetime of an entire tradition. “Living traditions” is a theme, not a dated era. Named artists are provided where documented; historical workshop artists are not assigned invented names. Pins identify representative centres and approximate coordinates. This is an educational geographic map, not a navigation or legal boundary reference.

Sources & image credits

Descriptions are original summaries of the linked sources. Image pages retain their own credits and reuse terms. Decorative line motifs are original schematic illustrations, not photographs or reproductions of historical works.

Map credit

India boundaries by the DataMeet India community, CC BY 4.0. The composite country geometry has been simplified and transformed to a local equirectangular drawing. No state boundaries are shown.

Project method

Research → select geographically varied examples → summarize eras, people and works → plot approximate locations → build searchable, keyboard-accessible interactions → verify browser behaviour. AI-assisted research, writing and coding; the student should review the material and disclose assistance as required by class rules.

Prepare your submission

Due: 21 October 2026, 10:00 AM IST. Aim to upload by 9:30 AM so a file or network problem does not make you late.

Your details are embedded in the downloaded copy.

Submission checklist

  1. Enter your details and choose Save submission HTML. Keep the downloaded file’s .html extension.
  2. Open that downloaded copy in Chrome or Edge. Test three pins, a search, a filter and the reset button. Disconnect from the internet and check that the map still works.
  3. Submit the HTML file through your teacher’s specified platform. If HTML uploads are blocked, put the file in a ZIP and upload that. A screenshot alone loses the interactivity.
  4. Re-download the uploaded file and open it once. Keep a second copy on a USB drive or your device for the classroom demo.

A 90-second demonstration

  1. 0–15 seconds: Explain that this map explores how place, patronage and community shape art.
  2. 15–40 seconds: Open Ajanta and point out its Buddhist cave murals. Open Konark and contrast painted storytelling with carved temple art.
  3. 40–65 seconds: Filter to Living traditions and show Madhubani or Majuli. Explain how art continues through community practice.
  4. 65–90 seconds: Reset, open Mumbai and explain that modern art developed through urban networks. Show a source link and conclude that Indian art has many regional centres.

Printing the page can provide a map plus the selected entry as a backup. It does not preserve the full interactive project. Review the twelve entries so you can explain them in your own words.
